Stage 3 · Grammar

Verbs you cannot watch happening

Some verbs describe a state, not an action. They behave differently.

Read these four sentences.
  • She is queuing outside the shop.
  • She believes shopping makes her happy.
  • They are transporting the goods by air.
  • That coat belongs to my brother.
Which of these verbs are never used in the continuous? Why not?
Some verbs describe things you can watch happening. Others describe things that are simply the case.

English divides verbs into two groups that behave differently. Dynamic verbs describe actions: things somebody does, which have a beginning, a middle and an end. State verbs describe conditions: what somebody thinks, feels, owns, senses or is. Because a state is not an activity that unfolds in front of you, English does not normally allow state verbs in the continuous form.

It is tempting to think this is about duration — that long things take the continuous and short things do not. It is not. Sleep lasts for hours and takes the continuous perfectly happily (She’s sleeping). Realize takes a fraction of a second and cannot (I’m realizing). The question is not how long it lasts but whether the subject is doing something or whether something is simply true of them.

The main state groups are worth learning as families rather than one by one: thinking and opinion (believe, think, know, understand, realize, mean, remember, agree), feelings and wanting (like, love, hate, prefer, want, need, mind), the senses (see, hear, smell, taste, feel, usually with can), possession and relationship (own, belong to, have, contain, cost, weigh), and being or appearing (be, seem, appear, look, sound, resemble).

The complication — and the reason this lesson exists rather than a simple list — is that a number of common verbs belong to both groups, with a different meaning in each. I think it’s expensive is an opinion and takes the simple; I’m thinking about buying it is a mental activity and takes the continuous. I have two brothers is possession; I’m having lunch is an activity. The form you choose tells your listener which meaning you intend, so this is not a technicality — it changes what you have said.

Before you look at the table: the tables below list the state groups and then the double-meaning verbs. As you read them, keep asking the one useful question: could I film somebody doing this? If not, the verb stays simple.
The two kinds of verb
KindWhat it describesContinuous?Example
Action (dynamic)something you can see happeningyesShe is queuing. He is buying a coat.
State — thinkingbelieve, think (= have an opinion), mean, realize, understand, recognizenoI believe you. I am believing you.
State — feeling and wantingprefer, want, like, need, hatenoWe prefer local shops.
State — havingown, belong, have (= possess), costnoIt belongs to her. It costs too much.
Three verbs change their meaning
VerbState — simpleAction — continuous
thinkI think it’s a bargain. (= my opinion)I’m thinking about buying it. (= mental activity)
haveShe has two phones. (= owns)She’s having a look at the offers. (= doing)
seeI see what you mean. (= understand)I’m seeing her on Friday. (= meeting)

The test. Ask yourself: could I film it? If you could film it, it is an action and the continuous is possible. If you could not — believing, owning, preferring — use the simple form.

Careful with think, have and see. These sit in both columns. The continuous does not just change the time; it changes the meaning.

The mistake to avoid. Not I am not understanding but I don’t understand. Not Are you wanting a bag? but Do you want a bag? State verbs take the present simple even when you are talking about right now.

Note. This does not stop state verbs going into the present perfect: I have known that for years, She has owned it since March recycled.

Full grammar reference — state verbs, and dynamic verbs that look like them

What it is

A state verb (also called a stative verb) describes a condition rather than an action: a thought, a feeling, a sense, a relationship or a possession. Because a state is not something you can watch happening and then stop, state verbs are normally used in the simple form and not in the continuous, in any tense.

What it means, and what it does

The distinction is about how English classifies the meaning, not about how long something lasts. Sleep lasts hours and takes the continuous (She’s sleeping); realize takes a second and does not (I’m realizing). What matters is whether the verb describes something the subject does or something that is simply the case.

When and why we use it

English divides verbs into two groups that behave differently. Dynamic verbs describe actions: things somebody does, which have a beginning, a middle and an end. State verbs describe conditions: what somebody thinks, feels, owns, senses or is. Because a state is not an activity that unfolds in front of you, English does not normally allow state verbs in the continuous form.

It is tempting to think this is about duration — that long things take the continuous and short things do not. It is not. Sleep lasts for hours and takes the continuous perfectly happily (She’s sleeping). Realize takes a fraction of a second and cannot (I’m realizing). The question is not how long it lasts but whether the subject is doing something or whether something is simply true of them.

The main state groups are worth learning as families rather than one by one: thinking and opinion (believe, think, know, understand, realize, mean, remember, agree), feelings and wanting (like, love, hate, prefer, want, need, mind), the senses (see, hear, smell, taste, feel, usually with can), possession and relationship (own, belong to, have, contain, cost, weigh), and being or appearing (be, seem, appear, look, sound, resemble).

The complication — and the reason this lesson exists rather than a simple list — is that a number of common verbs belong to both groups, with a different meaning in each. I think it’s expensive is an opinion and takes the simple; I’m thinking about buying it is a mental activity and takes the continuous. I have two brothers is possession; I’m having lunch is an activity. The form you choose tells your listener which meaning you intend, so this is not a technicality — it changes what you have said.

Typical situations

State verbs dominate any conversation where you give opinions, describe preferences, talk about what things cost or who owns what, or react to what you can see, hear and taste. Shopping, reviewing, negotiating and disagreeing are all built almost entirely out of them.

  • Thinking and opinion — believe, think (= have an opinion), suppose, doubt, know, understand, realize, remember, forget, mean, agree.I believe the price is fair. I don’t think so.
  • Feelings and wanting — like, love, hate, prefer, want, need, mind, wish.I prefer local shops. We don’t need another phone.
  • The senses, with can — see, hear, smell, taste, feel — the involuntary use, usually with can.I can hear something. This coffee tastes sour.
  • Possession and relationship — own, belong to, have (= possess), contain, include, consist of, cost, weigh.This coat belongs to my sister. It costs forty thousand tenge.
  • Appearance and being — be, seem, appear, look (= seem), resemble, sound.She seems convinced. That sounds like a bargain.

How it differs from similar structures

think = have an opinion (state) · be thinking = the mental activity of considering. I think you’re right vs I’m thinking about changing jobs.
have = own (state) · be having = experience or consume. She has a car vs She’s having a bad day.

How to build it

State verb: subject + simple form — I believe, she owns, they don’t want
Not: subject + be + state verb-ing — I am believing
Dynamic use of the same verb: subject + am / is / are + verb-ing — I’m thinking about it
AffirmativeI believe you. · She owns two shops.
NegativeI don’t believe it. · It doesn’t belong to me.
QuestionDo you believe her? · Does it cost much?
Short answersYes, I do. / No, it doesn’t.
In other tensesState verbs still take the perfect and the past: I have known that for years, She owned it then.
Dynamic pairI think it’s wrong (opinion) · I’m thinking about it (mental activity).

Usage notes and exceptions

  • Several verbs are both, with two different meanings. As a state they take the simple; as an activity they take the continuous. Learn them in pairs: think, have, see, taste, smell, feel, look, appear, weigh, expect.
  • Have: I have two brothers (possession, state) but I’m having lunch / a shower / a problem (activity).
  • See: I see what you mean (understand, state) but I’m seeing the manager at four (meeting, activity).
  • Taste / smell: The soup tastes salty (the quality it has) but He’s tasting the soup (what he is doing).
  • Be is a state, but the continuous is possible when it means behaving: You’re being unfair = you are behaving unfairly right now.
  • Some verbs allow the continuous in modern informal English for a temporary, emphatic effect — the well-known advertising line I’m loving it. It is not wrong, but at B1 in exams and writing keep love, like, want, need in the simple.

Watch out — the mistakes learners really make

  • I am believing you. → I believe you.Believe is a state: no continuous.
  • I am not understanding this word. → I don’t understand this word.Understand is a state, so the negative uses don’t.
  • Who is this bag belonging to? → Who does this bag belong to?Belong is a state; the question needs do / does.
  • I am wanting a refund. → I want a refund.Want stays simple even when the feeling is momentary.
  • She is having two sisters. → She has two sisters.Have meaning possess is a state.
  • The soup is tasting salty. → The soup tastes salty.Here taste describes a quality, not an action.

More examples in context

  • opinionI don’t think a special offer really saves you money.
  • mental activityI’m thinking of buying it second-hand.
  • possessionThat bag belongs to the woman in the queue.
  • costA guilt-free brand usually costs more.
  • sensesI can smell something burning.
  • action with a sense verbHe’s smelling the coffee before he buys it.
  • appearanceShe seems convinced by the argument.
  • behaviourStop it — you’re being ridiculous.
  • state in the perfectWe’ve owned this shop since 2018.
  • negative preferenceI don’t mind paying more if the workers are paid fairly.

A tip for remembering it

Try to picture the verb as a short film. If you can see somebody doing it — queuing, buying, tasting the soup — the continuous is available. If there is nothing to film because it is simply true inside somebody’s head or true of the world — believing, owning, costing — keep it simple.

Before you practise — the key rules

  1. State verbs describe conditions, not actions, and normally take the simple form only.
  2. The main groups are thinking, feeling and wanting, the senses, possession, and appearance.
  3. Negatives and questions use do / does, not be: I don’t understand, Does it cost much?
  4. Some verbs have a state meaning and an activity meaning; the continuous only fits the activity one.
  5. State verbs still work normally in the past and the present perfect — the restriction is on the continuous, not on the tense.
  6. At B1, keep love, like, want, need, believe, understand in the simple in writing and exams.

Stage 5 · Main input

Why we spend

Buy Nothing Day, and the guilt of a good deal.

Before you read: one day a year, some people ask everybody to buy absolutely nothing.

Could you go twenty-four hours without spending any money? Decide first, then read.

There is no right answer. This is your prediction — check at the end whether the text changed your mind.

Why we spend

One day a year, a small group of people stand in the busiest shops in the country and buy absolutely nothing. They think the rest of us should try it.

AEvery November the shops fill up. Prices fall, the windows say HALF-PRICE, and for a few days the whole country seems to be shopping. Some people queue outside the doors all night in the run-up to Christmas. Others buy on credit and only understand what they have spent when the bill arrives in January. In Britain alone, shoppers spend around nine billion pounds in that single week.

BThen, on the busiest shopping day of the year, a small group of people stand in the same shopping centres holding signs. They are not buying anything. It is Buy Nothing Day, and they want the rest of us to stop for twenty-four hours and think. The movement started in Canada in 1992 and now appears in more than sixty-five countries.

C“We believe shopping makes us happy,” says Lewis Castle, who has been part of the movement since 2013. “It doesn’t. Look at what happens afterwards.” He means the money people owe, and he means the planet: the richest fifth of the world’s population consumes far more than its fair share of the world’s resources, and moving goods around the world by air is one of the most harmful parts of the whole system.

DShops understand exactly how a bargain feels. A special offer does not simply mean a lower price; it means you were clever. Researchers who study consumer behaviour call this the deal effect, and it explains something strange: people come home with items they do not need, feel briefly pleased, and admit weeks later that they never wanted them at all. What follows has a plainer name. Guilt.

EGuilt sells too. The current trend is guilt-free brands — a phone you can repair, a shirt made by workers who are paid properly, a coffee that promises to protect the forest it came from. Some shoppers are convinced this is real progress, and it is not hard to see why: a company that publishes what it pays its workers is doing something its competitors are not. Others think it is an excuse. Buy the guilt-free version, they argue, and you never have to ask the harder question.

FThat question is not what you buy. It is why. Castle does not tell anybody to stop shopping for ever, and he does not pretend that one day in November changes anything. He says something much smaller and, he thinks, more useful. For twenty-four hours, you notice how often your hand goes to your pocket — and you find out how much of it you actually wanted.

Written for this course. Figures on consumption and household debt are drawn from published UN Environment Programme and OECD reporting.
